To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

24-hour ambulation blood pressure recordings, obtained with a noninvasive device, are able to discriminate better among patients with different target organ damage than traditional sphygmomanometer readings, and that blood pressure variability, as assessed by these recordings, is as important as blood-pressure mean values in the evaluation of cardiovascular risk in patients with hypertension.

1) 24-hour ambulator blood pressure monitoring, by overcoming some limitations inherent in isolated cuff measurements, may improve diagnostic approach to hypertension, 2) 24-hour blood pressures are better able to discriminate among hypertensive patients with different degrees and types of target organ damage, 3) 24-hour intraarterial recordings have shown that blood pressure variability may have a role in the assessment of target organ damage.

24-hour ambulatorily monitored blood pressure is a better predictor of target organ damage in hypertensives than is the office blood pressure, and that blood pressure variability, as measured by 24-hour blood pressures, is as important as the mean blood pressure in the assessment of the cardiovascular complications of hypertension.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method to assess the cardiovascular effects of drugs, which are not detectable by means of the conventional clinical approach to drug evaluation.
a better definition of the diagnostic value of blood pressure monitoring in hypertensive patients, both in the clinical setting and in research.
the study of blood pressure variability and its relation to the presence of cardiovascular complications in hypertensive patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of ambulatory blood pressure recordings is not only feasible but may also improve the clinical management of hypertensive patients.
the 24-hour ambulatorily recorded blood pressure is the most accurate method to assess the cardiovascular risk of hypertensive patients.

24-hour ambulant blood pressure monitoring may be a very useful tool in the management of hypertensive patients, but that its role should be carefully assessed in large clinical trials before being considered a standard approach to the diagnosis and management of arterial hypertension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of 24 hour blood pressure monitoring in hypertensive patients is useful in the diagnosis and follow-up of the disease, but it is not a substitute for the traditional cuff measurements.
the ambulatory blood pressure monitor (ABPM) can be an important tool for the evaluation and management of patients with hypertension.
24-hour ambulant blood pressure monitoring may provide a more accurate assessment of the cardiovascular risk of hypertensive patients than conventional sphygmomanometer measurements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of noninvasive ambulatory blood pressure monitors can be a very helpful tool in the assessment of patients with hypertension and in the evaluation of antihypertensive therapy.
24-hour ambulant blood pressure recordings are superior to isolated sphygmomaniometric measurements in the evaluation of hypertensive patients.
24-hour ambulant blood pressure monitoring may improve the diagnostic approach and the follow-up of hypertensive patients.
